text: Τοὺς ἐν αἰῶσι καὶ χρόνοις φυσικῶς περιγράφον. Incipit hic Turr. Tantis desideratis: nec placet, quod vocem περιγράφον, reddit, circumscribit et terminat: altera enim ac prior vox, una sufficit, verumque sensum Græcæ illius reddit, prout a Cicerone, Cæsare, aliisque usurpatur, relatis a Bud. in Comm. Est ergo ἄρρητον τὸ τῆς οἰκονομίας μυστήριον, arcanum nullis verbis explicabile; et ut reddit ipse Turr. nullos explicatus habens; quod ævum omne ac sæculum, et qui eis continentur, natura circumscribat; tanquam scilicet eis eminens, id est, excludat, e numero auferat. Similis lapsus notatus n. 1, in vocibus περιγράφειν et περιορίζειν.
anchorLine: φον (m), συγχεῖν μηχανώμενοι μυστήριον
en: 'Those in ages and times, circumscribed by nature.' Here Turrianus begins. In so much that is missing [in his version]: nor does it please me that he rendered the word περιγράφον as 'circumscribes and limits'; for the first word, being the earlier, is sufficient on its own and gives the true sense of that Greek word, as used by Cicero, Caesar and others, as cited by Budaeus in his Commentaries. So the mystery of the economy is ἄρρητον, a secret that cannot be explained in words; and as Turrianus himself rendered it, 'having no explanations'; because nature circumscribes every age and era and what is contained in them, as though standing above them, that is, excluding them and removing them from the number. A similar slip is noted at no. 1, in the words περιγράφειν and περιορίζειν.

text: Ἀλλ' ἄνωθεν καὶ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς συνουσιωμένην αὐτῷ. Turr. Sed superne et a principio deferens copulavit eam secum secundum substantiam: quasi unum Valentini errorem hæc suffigant, delati e cœlo corporis, cœlestisque materiæ, non ex nobis assumpti; quod toto cœla a Maximi mente abest. Τὸ, ἄνωθεν, ut hic sumendum, ipsa Maximi correctio notat, ἢ οὐδὲ λαβών, quæ nec Turriano defuit, dum reddit, aut neque sumpsit. Sumpsit certe, etsi superne, sive e cœlo devexit. Ἄνωθεν ergo, ipsum est quod ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, a principio, ex ipsa origine ac processione; quomodo usurpavit Greg. in hoc carmine, Ὧν τὸ μὲν ἦεν ἄνωθεν· Quorum hoc quidem erat a principio, ex origine; uti etiam Demosth. τὸ συνουσιωμένην, secundum substantiam unitam; longe est a viro theologo. συνουσιασμός, Eutychianorum est et Severianorum; unitio secundum substantiam, et substantialis, sive etiam naturalis, Christi Ecclesiæ, auctore præsertim Cyrillo. Illud, substantiarum confusio, altera ab altera absorpta, vel etiam ex ambabus una tertia effecta, uti passim Maximus exprimit, et qui eam confundentium hæresim impugnant: istud, vera essentiarum seu naturarum, καθ' ὑπόστασιν, sustinendi ratione (quæ et post unitionem distinctionem retineant, ac quod unaquæque nata est) copulatio. Nec in re sic trita morandum, nisi quantum adegit tanta illa superioris interpretis vere ἀθεόλογος; oscitantia.
anchorLine: …συνουσιωμένην αὐτῷ (n) κατενέχθη…
en: 'But from above and from the beginning united in substance with him.' Turrianus has: 'But bringing it from above and from the beginning he joined it to himself according to substance', as though these words supported the one error of Valentinus, of a body brought down from heaven and of heavenly matter, not taken from us; which is utterly far from Maximus's mind. That ἄνωθεν must be taken as here [rendered] is shown by Maximus's own correction, 'or not having taken', which Turrianus did not lack either when he renders 'or did not take'. He certainly took it, even if he brought it down from above, that is from heaven. So ἄνωθεν is the same as ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, 'from the beginning', from the very origin and procession, as Gregory uses it in his poem, 'of which one was from above', that is 'from the beginning, from the origin'; so too Demosthenes. The word συνουσιωμένην, 'united in substance', is far from the theologian. συνουσιασμός belongs to the Eutychians and Severians: a union according to substance, and substantial or even natural, of Christ and the Church, especially according to Cyril. The one [sense] is a confusion of substances, one swallowed by the other, or even a third made from both, as Maximus everywhere expresses it and as those who oppose the heresy of the confounders do; the other is a union of true essences or natures, according to hypostasis, on the principle of sustaining them (which retain their distinction even after the union, and what each was born to be). One need not linger over so well-worn a matter, except so far as that great carelessness of the earlier translator, truly lacking sound theology, compelled it.

anchorLine: …οὔτε ἐστιν τί ἐστιν (ο). Διὰ τοι τοῦτο…
en: Θέσις: Turrianus rightly has 'Positio' (positing), to which ἀφαίρεσις (removal) is opposed, as also 'to do philosophy about God by positing' as against 'by removal', that is by affirming and by denying; on which matter see the same Dionysius, On Mystical Theology, Lansel[ottus]. Ἀφαίρεσις is not rendered well as 'eminentia' in Dionysius, as neither is Cordier's 'situs'. But there are other errors in Dionysius and in their scholia that I must correct.

text: Καλοφροσύνης. Vox paulo rarior. Hesych. τὸ καλόφρον affert, explicanda voce εὔφρων, uti etiam vocem αἰδέσιμος: huncque vel maxime ejus sensum putem hic spectasse Maximum, prout vox αἰδέσιμος active etiam sumitur; quam ejus significationem confirmavi ex Orig. in ejus Catena in Genesim, ubi illi sermo est de Rebecca. Catena hæc exiguis laboribus undecunque licuit ex omnibus Origenianis in Scripturam mihi collecta, notisque illustrata, in Huetii manibus prælum exspectat: nec quia symbolæ sunt, sic elevandæ, ut jam vir doctus insinuavit. Videmus quanta fide in aliis excerptæ ejusmodi symbolæ, ipsoque adeo Origene, in quibus libri integri exstant, ut inde libros aliquot Cyrilli in Joannem supplere licuerit. Breviant plerumque, quandoque etiam, servata sententia, tantisper verba mutant, qui hoc scribendi genus, inter Græcos maxime, secuti sunt: quo fit ut in secundis habenda sint ejus generis scripta, non ut pene nulla; mihi haud raro interpolatis Rufino ejusque affusis furfuribus ad fidem auctorumque censum potiora. Sed hæc obiter. Ad rem quod attinet, prætexebant pietatem Eutychiani et Monothelitæ, quasi vererentur illi quidem, nec admissa distinctione solveretur naturarum unitio; hi vero, ne contrarias in Christo voluntates ac peccatum inducerent, si et humana præditum voluntate dicerent. Quæ maxime Sergii cavillatio fuit, ejusque discipuli Macarii Antiocheni. Reddi itaque possit, animi probitas, verecundia ac pudor, cautio ac timor, et si quid ejusmodi est: Turr. bellam prudentiam reddit: possit et sapientiam. Dictum καλοφροσύνης, quasi ironice et per ἀντίφρασιν, pro κακοφροσύνης, quod est malitia, mentis, perversitas.
anchorLine: σύνης (p), ταύτην τινὲς προφασίζονται· καὶ τὸν
en: 'Καλοφροσύνης': a somewhat rare word. Hesychius offers τὸ καλόφρον, explained by the word εὔφρων, as also the word αἰδέσιμος; and I think Maximus had chiefly this sense in view here, as αἰδέσιμος is also taken actively; I confirmed that meaning from Origen in his Catena on Genesis, where he speaks of Rebecca. This Catena, gathered by me with modest labour from all the Origenian material on Scripture wherever possible, and annotated, awaits the press in Huet's hands; nor, because they are mere excerpts, should they be belittled, as a learned man has already hinted. We see with what fidelity such excerpts were made elsewhere, even from Origen himself, where whole books survive, so that several books of Cyril on John could be supplied from them. Those who follow this kind of writing, chiefly among the Greeks, often abridge and sometimes, keeping the sense, change the wording for a while; so such writings are to be counted second-rank, not as nearly worthless; to me they are often preferable to texts interpolated by Rufinus and sprinkled with his chaff, as regards faithfulness and the weight of authors. But that is by the way. As to the point at hand: the Eutychians and Monothelites put forward piety as a pretext, as if they feared that, once a distinction was admitted, the union of the natures would be dissolved; and the latter, lest they introduce contrary wills in Christ and sin, if they said he was endowed with a human will as well. This was above all the quibble of Sergius and of his disciple Macarius of Antioch. It can therefore be rendered 'uprightness of mind, modesty and shame, caution and fear', and whatever is of that kind; Turrianus renders it 'bellam prudentiam' ['fine prudence']; 'wisdom' also could be used. [The Greek] was said of καλοφροσύνη as if ironically and by antiphrasis, for κακοφροσύνη, that is malice, malignity of mind, perversity.

en: Fr. [reads]: 'That the flesh too is God, by its union with the Word; and its natural properties have become divine by union and growth together with him.' [Latin gloss:] that the flesh is God by union with the Word, and that its natural properties are made divine by union and cohesion with him.

text: Μεγίστης ἔχεται διανοίας. Dionysii intelligentiæ cohæreret; eumdem sensum altissimum habet. Ac certe carnis Christi communitatem hanc operationis ac virtutis cum Verbo ac unitione ad ipsum, nedum in propria specie, sed et in mystica benedictione, ut vocat, seu Eucharistia, nemo Patrum plenius Cyrillo altiusque exsecutus est, prorsus consentanee ac proxime Dionysio, sive ipsum Cyrillus legit, sive eamdem ac ille ecclesiasticam doctrinam ac traditionem exposuit: cujus etiam multa mihi relata ac stylo ornata in Biblioth. PP. concionat. ad diem festum Corporis Christi. Non satis expedite Turr., maximam sententiam Patris continet.
anchorLine: τούτου Πατρὸς μεγίστης ἔχεται διανοίας (q).
en: 'Holds to a very great thought.' It coheres with the understanding of Dionysius; it has the same most exalted sense. And certainly, as to this communion of Christ's flesh in operation and power with the Word and by union with him, not only in its proper kind but also in 'mystical blessing', as he calls it, that is the Eucharist, no Father has treated it more fully and more deeply than Cyril, in complete agreement and closest accord with Dionysius, whether Cyril read Dionysius himself or set out the same ecclesiastical doctrine and tradition as he; many of Cyril's words on this I have reported, adorned with style, in the Bibliotheca Patrum, in the sermon for the feast of Corpus Christi. Turrianus renders it not very clearly; it contains the Father's greatest thought.

text: Ὧ τὰ ἐκεῖθεν συνεφιλοσόφησε. Exciderunt hæc verba doctissimo interpreti Billio, solita elegantia reddituro. Turr. qua de iis, quæ illic sunt, philosophatus est. Durum mihi, carne philosophari de cœlestibus et æternis; de rebus scilicet ævi futuri. Hæc enim sunt τὰ ἐκεῖ, ut et τὰ ἐνταῦθα, quæ sunt ævi præsentis. Spiritu potius et animo de illo philosophamur, etsi cum carne, illaque ei socia ac subministra, seu instrumento ejus philosophiæ; qua ipsa virtutibus componitur, ac ratione regitur.
anchorLine: ἀπολαβοῦσα, ᾧ τὰ ἐκεῖθεν συνεφιλοσόφησεν (r).
en: 'With which he philosophised on the things from there.' These words escaped the very learned translator Billy, who would otherwise have rendered them with his usual elegance. Turrianus has 'by which he philosophised about the things that are there'. It is hard for me [to accept] philosophising with the flesh about heavenly and eternal things, that is, about the things of the age to come. For these are τὰ ἐκεῖ ('the things there'), as τὰ ἐνταῦθα are 'the things here', which belong to the present age. We philosophise about it rather with spirit and mind, even if with the flesh, which is its companion and servant, or the instrument of that philosophy; and the flesh itself is ordered by the virtues and governed by reason.

text: Καὶ ὁ ὑπὸ τοῦ συγγενοῦς μαρτυρούμενος Πνεύματος. Aliam Maximus, aut pleniorem habuit Greg. litteram cum hæc modo solum habeat, ἐκεῖθεν γὰρ ὁ μαρτυρούμενος. Inde enim cui testimonium perhibebatur.

text: Ἀλλ' ἀμέτοχος πάντῃ. Legit Turr. ἀλλὰ μέτοχος, quod et habuit Geras. Blacchi cod. Venet. aperto nimis errore. Reddit itaque, sed potius participans omnino secundum substantiam ab omni natura differt. Quæ ipsa aperte pugnant. Non enim differt natura a natura, seu ab ea distinguitur, quod participet, sed quod non participet, sitque quo participent personæ et ὑποστάσεις, ipsa non participans. Quo fit ut, si una Christus natura est, uti operatio, nihil sit eorum ex quibus constitutus est, id est, nec Deus, nec homo, nec cum Patre nec nobiscum communicet. Quod argumentum, uti alibi passim, sic hic quoque Maximus vexat: nec debuit vir theologus re tam proclivi ab ejus deviare sententia, ac quod ab omni abhorret sacra profanaque philosophia, ex nota elisionis male omissa, festinante Antiquarii calamo, deroquere.
anchorLine: ἀλλ' ἀμέτοχος, πάντῃ (t) κατ' οὐσίαν πρὸς πάσας
en: 'But wholly without participation.' Turrianus read ἀλλὰ μέτοχος, 'but participating', which Geras also had, and the Venice codex of Blacchus, by an obvious error. So he renders it, 'but rather participating, wholly according to substance, it differs from every nature'. These things plainly contradict one another. For one nature does not differ from another, or is not distinguished from it, because it participates, but because it does not participate, and it is that in which persons and hypostases participate, itself not participating. Hence, if Christ is one nature, like his operation, he is none of the things from which he is composed, that is, he would be neither God nor man, and would not communicate with the Father or with us. This argument Maximus presses, as elsewhere throughout; the theologian should not have departed from his own meaning in so easy a matter, and from what every sound sacred or profane philosophy abhors, by an omitted elision-mark, [owing to] the hasty pen of the copyist, [to] ...  [the last word, 'deroquere', is unclear in the scan].

text: Ἵν' ἐκ τούτου οὐ μεσίτας Θεοῦ μᾶλλον. Addidi negantem particulam, quod necessario sensus exposcit. Quid enim sensus, quod absque illa habent Græca, et reddit Turr. ut hinc vos magis sequestros Dei, quam imitatores præstetis. Imo certe contrarium. Significat enim episcopos pro munere, et qua divinis dotibus eo sublimes fulgent, non tam ad Deum intercedere (quanquam et hoc eorum muneris est) quam ipsos quoque (quod pene divinius videatur) Dei imitatione divina præbere ac perficere; quippe gradu ipso τελειωτικούς, sub summo hierarcha Christo, ea functione ejusque vicarios. Hoc enim est quod sequitur, Non solum ejus in omnem illustrationem ac misericordiam habitu consecuti ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄξια παρέχοντες: verum etiam pro dignitatis munere præbentes. Ubi Turr. ἄξια legit, sed digna etiam ei præbentes: male vero τὸ, ei, quasi eos digna Deo præbere dicat Maximus, quod prorsus abhorret, vel si ἄξια demus eum scripsisse. Præbent certe illi populis ἄξια, in hoc illis comparata dignitate; vel etiam ἄξια, ut quisque dignus est accipere. Sed illud primum longe aptius. Continere habitu, vel ea habitu nactos esse, privatorum potius est. Scripserit et ipse Turr. eis, etsi ita illi prelum erravit.
anchorLine: διόρθωσιν· Ἵν' ἐκ τούτου μεσίτας Θεοῦ μᾶλλον (u),
en: 'So that from this you may be mediators of God rather [than ...]'. I have added the negating particle, which the sense necessarily demands. For what sense is there, since the Greek has it without that, and Turrianus renders it 'that from this you may show yourselves rather as God's go-betweens than as imitators'? On the contrary, surely. For [Maximus] means that bishops, by their office and by the divine gifts by which they shine on high, do not so much intercede with God (though that too is part of their office) as also (which may seem almost more divine) bring about and perfect divine things in others by imitation of God, being in that very rank 'perfecters' under Christ the supreme hierarch, and his vicars in that function. For this is what follows: 'having attained not only the state of illumination and mercy that belongs to him, but also supplying worthy things'; indeed supplying them according to the dignity of their office. Where Turrianus reads ἄξια, but [translates] 'supplying worthy things to him': the 'to him' is wrong, as if Maximus said they supply God with worthy things, which he utterly rejects, even if we grant that he wrote ἄξια. They certainly supply the peoples with ἄξια, a dignity suited to them in this; or else ἄξια, as each is worthy to receive. But the first sense is far more apt. 'Containing by a habit', or 'having obtained them by a habit', is more characteristic of private persons. Turrianus himself may have written 'to them', even if the press erred so.

text: indicare scriptam epistolam in ipsa Siciliæ insula, cum jam illud diverticulum sibi Monothelitæ quæsissent, ut et unam et duas in Christo operationes ponerent: quam conati sunt Maximo affingere, ac postea in eam illum trahere pro primi ejus exilii tempore, quando et ipsi Eugenii apocrisiarii in eam novam fidem sunt inducti. Videtur itaque Maximus voluisse, ut hanc Siculi ejus illibatæ fidei certum pignus haberent, ac cunctis illius obtrectatoribus opponerent, in qua non perinde cavillari liberum esset, ac in eis quæ ore tenus ad eos locutus esset. Sicque animo insinuat in prooemio. Titulus quem repræsentat Turr. Epistola sancti Maximi ad sanctos Patres præpositos et monachos, et populos catholicos insulæ Siciliæ habitatores, contra eos qui unam in Christo operationem ponunt, ab Antiquario palam adjectus est; quem ex aliis repræsento, ipsa sit Maximo apposita ἐπιγραφή: magis proinde probanda; uti etiam quam repræsento ex Dufrenii Codice ad Quæst. in Scripturam.
anchorLine: (call stands on p-0072: Τοῖς κατὰ τήνδε τὴν Σικελῶν (v) φιλόχριστον)
en: [The pronoun] seems to indicate a letter written in Sicily itself, when the Monothelites had already sought that refuge for themselves, so as to posit both one and two operations in Christ: which they tried to attribute to Maximus, and afterwards to drag him into it at the time of his first exile, when even Eugenius's apocrisiaries were led into that new faith. So Maximus seems to have wished that the Sicilians should have this as a sure pledge of his unblemished faith, and set it against all his detractors, since in it there was no such freedom for quibbling as in what he had said to them by word of mouth. And so he hints in the preface. The title Turrianus gives, 'Letter of Saint Maximus to the holy Fathers, superiors and monks, and the Catholic peoples inhabiting the island of Sicily, against those who posit one operation in Christ', was openly added by a copyist; the one I give from others is the very inscription attached by Maximus, and so is the more to be approved; as is also the one I give from the Dufresne codex of the Questions on Scripture.

text: Τῶν ἀντιῤῥόπων καὶ ἐναντίων δογμάτων ὑπόληψις. Sic Maximus novam Monothelitarum opinionem argute vocat, seu illorum damnatæ jam hæresis commentum et evasionem. Una itaque voluntate et operatione, una cum Ecthesi, Joanni IV ac cunctis Occident. necnon Sophronio Hierosolymorum episcopo, reprobata, hoc novatoribus succurrit, ut tanquam ἀντίῤῥοπον (æquivalens, par, æquale) unam, duasque eas dicerent: quod tamen Maximus contrarium esse contendit; ac ejusmodi, ut alterum alterum evertat. Non recte itaque Turr. Nunquam me sensisse aut suspicatum esse de contrariis et repugnantibus dogmatibus, ut et infra, περὶ τῶν ἀντιῤῥόπων οὑτωσὶ καὶ ἐναντίων δογμάτων: de contrariis dogmatibus: ac si ambæ voces essent ejusdem prorsus significationis; quod longe est a vera Gramm. ἀντίῤῥοπον enim, ἰσόῤῥοπον est Suid. ἴσον, ἰσόσταθμον, ἰσόζυγον Hesych. quod perinde lancem trahit, ejusdemque ponderis est; a quo certe procul contrarii ratio est. Nec ii vero longe abesse a Monothelitarum illo genio videantur, qui nuper damnatarum Romæ propositionum acrius defensores, ac cum suo antistite, parum Thomistarum scholæ faventes, atque errantium albo, primo ipso ordine ascribentes, nunc sibi in uno Thoma, velut ei semper militaverint, præsidium quærunt: ac utinam vere quærant, ac quidquid de gratia senserint, ad illius normam, hinc plane erroris ac notæ perpetuo securi, componant. Ineptiunt enim, ni vere ἀσεβοῦντας quis malit dicere, nec magis Angelico præceptori quam ipsi Sedi apostolicæ, inque ea nuper præsidenti Alexandro VII injurii sunt, qui vel scioli vel procaces, vel invidi ac malevoli, obtinente ejus ipsius testimonio, damnatam sancti Thomæ ac Thomistarum in Jansenianam doctrinam deblaterant, aut etiam chartis illinunt atque evulgant.
anchorLine: δογμάτων ὑπόληψις (x). Οὐδὲ γὰρ μίαν ἐν ταὐτῷ
en: 'The supposition of counterbalancing and contrary doctrines.' So Maximus cleverly names the new opinion of the Monothelites, that is, the contrivance and evasion of their already condemned heresy. With one will and one operation rejected, together with the Ecthesis, by John IV and all the West, and by Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, this expedient helped the innovators: that they might say 'one' and 'two' of them as though ἀντίῤῥοπον ('equivalent, equal, level'); which Maximus nevertheless contends is contrary, and of such a kind that the one overturns the other. So Turrianus is wrong in 'that I never thought or suspected of contrary and conflicting doctrines', as also below, 'on the ἀντίῤῥοπα, thus and contrary doctrines': as if the two words had the same meaning, which is far from true grammar. For ἀντίῤῥοπον is the same as ἰσόῤῥοπον, Suidas; 'equal, of equal weight, equally yoked', Hesychius: it tips the scale just alike and is of the same weight; the idea of contrary is far from it. Nor do those seem to stand far from that Monothelite temper who, as recent vehement defenders of the propositions condemned at Rome, and little favouring the school of the Thomists, enrol themselves in the list of the erring in the very first rank, and now seek protection in Thomas alone, as though they had always served under him: would that they did truly seek it, and bring whatever they think about grace into line with his norm, thus safe for ever from error and censure. For they talk nonsense, unless one would rather call them truly impious, and they wrong the Angelic Doctor no more than the Apostolic See itself, and in it Alexander VII, then presiding, they who, whether smatterers or insolent or envious and spiteful, with his own testimony in their favour, babble about the condemned doctrine of St Thomas and the Thomists against the Jansenist doctrine, or even smear it on pages and publish it.

text: Φύσιν τε λέγω καὶ ὑπόστασιν. Istud, quod superioris explicatio est, τοῦ καθ' ἑκατέραν, secundum utramque naturam scilicet et personam; Turr. velut absolutum facit relatum ad ὑπογράφοντες;, quo mihi ejus propositio non ferenda videtur, dum sic scribit, quasi Maximi sententiam reddens. Describentes, inquam, Filium esse naturam et hypostasim, quod est ab Ecclesia alienum. Ego non sic didici, nec me docuit Maximus; imo hunc Ecclesiæ catholicæ sensum accepi: nulla enim naturæ et hypostasis in Filio opposi io, ut non Catholice utrumque dici debeat, etsi idem duntaxat ratione naturæ cum Patre communicet, non ratione personæ; unumque hoc alienum dicat Maximus ab Ecclesia catholica, id est, cum eo communicare ratione utriusque, quod est personalem amborum oppositionem, ac proinde distinctionem, Sabelliano errore, tollere. Sic pronum in theologia, ex verbis incaute prolatis, in hæresim incidere, aut certe hæreticam pro Catholica propositionem dare.
anchorLine: νοῦντα, φύσιν τε λέγω καὶ ὑπόστασιν (y), τὸν Υἱὸν
en: 'I say nature and hypostasis.' This, which is an explanation of the preceding, [is of] τοῦ καθ' ἑκατέραν, that is 'according to each, nature and person'; Turrianus makes it as if absolute, relating it to ὑπογράφοντες, so that his proposition seems to me intolerable when he writes thus, as though rendering Maximus's meaning: 'Describing, I say, the Son to be nature and hypostasis', which is foreign to the Church. I did not learn it so, nor did Maximus teach me; on the contrary I took this to be the sense of the Catholic Church: for there is no opposition of nature and hypostasis in the Son, such that each could not be said in a Catholic way, although he communicates with the Father only in respect of nature, not of person; and the one thing Maximus calls foreign to the Catholic Church is to communicate with him in respect of both, which is to remove, by the Sabellian error, the personal opposition of the two and hence the distinction. So it is easy in theology to fall into heresy from incautiously uttered words, or at least to give a heretical proposition for a Catholic one.

text: Τῇ δὲ ἀχράντῳ Μητρί. Turr. quod est adversative, quasi conjunctive ponit, et cum Matre Virgine; quod forte error typorum est, pro, sed; ut et quod paulo post sequitur, impugnando tertiam illam totius seu personæ operationem, ὅπερ ἀδύνατον: quod est possibile, pro impossibile. Potuit Jac. Gretseri edendo sodalis posthumum hoc opus, sedulior opera elucere.
anchorLine: μὲν Πατρί· τῇ δὲ ἀχράντῳ μητρὶ (z) κοινωνεῖν κατὰ
en: 'But to the immaculate Mother.' Turrianus, which is adversative, puts as though conjunctive, 'and with the Virgin Mother'; which is perhaps a printers' error, for 'but'; as also what follows a little later, in refuting that third operation of the whole or of the person, ὅπερ ἀδύνατον ['which is impossible'], [he renders] 'which is possible', for 'impossible'. The posthumous work of the associate of Jacob Gretser who edited it could have shone forth with more diligent care.
